title: Plant Physiology: Water, Transport and Responses
description: The mechanism layer behind the Core plant topics for IGCSE Biology 0610: osmosis in water-potential terms, xylem structure, transpiration pull, translocation, limiting factors of photosynthesis, and how auxin controls tropic responses.

notes.heading: Where This Topic Sits + Osmosis in Water-Potential Terms
notes.body:
📌 Where this topic sits
The Core plant topics — diffusion and osmosis, photosynthesis, and plant transport — tell you WHAT moves in a plant. This topic is the mechanism layer: the Supplement objectives that explain HOW and WHY, in the vocabulary Extended mark schemes are written in. It also carries Core content (tropic responses), which is why it has no core/extended tag.

📌 Definition (Supplement 3.2.7)
**Osmosis** is the **net movement of water molecules** from a region of **higher water potential** to a region of **lower water potential**, through a **partially permeable membrane**.
**Water potential** measures the tendency of water molecules to move: pure water has the HIGHEST water potential, and dissolving solutes in water LOWERS its water potential. A concentrated solution therefore has a LOW water potential.

🔑 What the examiner wants
Quote the definition with all three elements: net movement of water, higher → lower water potential, partially permeable membrane. 'From dilute to concentrated' is the Core phrasing; the Supplement answer must use water potential. The basic osmosis practicals (potato cylinders, dialysis tubing) are covered in the Core diffusion and osmosis topic.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying a concentrated solution has a 'high water potential'. It is LOW — solutes lower the water potential. Water moves TOWARDS the concentrated solution, so that side must be the low-water-potential side.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Pure water = highest water potential; solutes lower it.
• Water flows down the water-potential gradient through a partially permeable membrane.

notes.heading: Turgid, Flaccid, Plasmolysed: Immersion Results Explained
notes.body:
📌 The three states of a plant cell (Supplement 3.2.8)
• **Turgid** — the surrounding solution has a HIGHER water potential than the cell sap → water ENTERS by osmosis → the vacuole swells and pushes the cytoplasm against the cell wall. The outward push on the wall is **turgor pressure**; the wall resists, so the cell is firm.
• **Flaccid** — the water potentials are EQUAL → no net movement of water → turgor pressure is lost and the cell goes limp.
• **Plasmolysed** — the surrounding solution has a LOWER water potential → water LEAVES by osmosis → the vacuole shrinks and the cell membrane pulls away from the cell wall. This state is called **plasmolysis**.

🔑 The importance of water potential (Supplement 3.2.9)
• Water uptake keeps cells turgid, and turgor pressure supports non-woody stems and holds leaves flat to the light.
• Water loss past the flaccid point is **wilting**: the whole tissue sags because its cells can no longer press against their walls.

💡 Worked Example
A potato cylinder gains mass in distilled water (higher water potential outside → water in → cells more turgid) and loses mass in concentrated salt solution (lower water potential outside → water out → cells flaccid, then plasmolysed). The point of no mass change is where the two water potentials are equal.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying an animal cell 'plasmolyses'. Animal cells have no cell wall: in pure water they BURST, and in concentrated solution they SHRIVEL. Plasmolysis — the membrane pulling away from the wall — is plant-only vocabulary.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Higher water potential outside → water in → turgid (turgor pressure).
• Lower water potential outside → water out → flaccid → plasmolysed.

illustration.alt: Three plant cells side by side showing turgid, flaccid and plasmolysed states, with arrows showing water entering, in balance, or leaving, decided by the water potential outside.
illustration.caption: The direction of osmosis is set by which side has the higher water potential: water enters and the cell becomes turgid, balances and the cell is flaccid, or leaves and the cell is plasmolysed.

notes.heading: Xylem: Structure Fitted to Function (Supplement 8.1.3)
notes.body:
📌 The three structural features
Xylem vessels are built from dead cells joined end to end, and every feature matches the job of carrying water up the plant:
• **Thick lignified walls** — **lignin** is a tough, waterproof material deposited in the wall. It strengthens the vessel so it does not collapse inwards when tension (a pull) develops inside, and it waterproofs the wall so water does not leak out sideways.
• **No cell contents** — no cytoplasm, nucleus or organelles remain, leaving a wide, empty lumen so water flows with little resistance.
• **No cross walls (end walls)** — the walls between neighbouring cells break down, so the vessels form **continuous tubes** running from root to leaf.

🔑 How to earn the marks
'Describe how xylem is adapted' questions want each feature LINKED to its function: 'lignified walls, SO the vessel resists collapse under tension'; 'no end walls, SO the water column is continuous'. An unlinked list of features scores only part of the marks.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Confusing xylem with phloem. Phloem sieve tube elements are LIVING and keep their end walls as perforated sieve plates. Xylem cells are dead, hollow and have no end walls at all.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Lignified walls, empty lumen, continuous tube.
• Xylem = dead; phloem = living.
• The pathway of water through root and leaf is covered in the Core plant transport topic.

notes.heading: Transpiration: the Mechanism, the Factors, and Wilting (Supplement 8.3)
notes.body:
📌 The mechanism
**Transpiration** is the loss of water vapour from the leaves: water evaporates from the surfaces of mesophyll cells into the internal air spaces, then diffuses out through the stomata. The rate depends on the **surface area of the air spaces** and on the **size and number of stomata**.
Evaporation from the mesophyll pulls more water across from the xylem. Because water molecules are **cohesive** (they stick together), that pull — the **transpiration pull** — drags a continuous column of water molecules up the xylem from the roots.

🔑 Explaining the three environmental factors (Supplement 8.3.6)
• **Temperature rises** → water molecules gain kinetic energy → evaporation from mesophyll surfaces is faster → transpiration faster.
• **Wind speed rises** → humid air is swept away from the leaf surface → the diffusion gradient between the air spaces and the outside stays steep → faster loss of water vapour.
• **Humidity rises** → the air outside already holds a lot of water vapour → the gradient between inside and outside the leaf is shallow → transpiration SLOWER.

🔑 Wilting — how and why (Supplement 8.3.7)
If transpiration exceeds water uptake, cells lose turgor and the leaves and young stems go limp — that is wilting. It is not pure damage: wilted leaves hang down, so less surface is exposed to the sun, and flaccid guard cells close the stomata, both of which reduce further water loss.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Learning only 'hot and windy = faster'. Exam questions love the humid, still day: HIGH humidity and LOW wind both slow transpiration, for the same gradient reason. Give the gradient explanation, not just 'less water is lost'.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Evaporation from mesophyll → diffusion through stomata; the pull passes down a cohesive water column.
• Faster: high temperature, high wind speed, LOW humidity.
• Wilting = turgor loss when loss exceeds uptake; it also protects the plant.

notes.heading: Translocation: Sources and Sinks (Supplement 8.4)
notes.body:
📌 Definition
**Translocation** is the movement of **sucrose and amino acids** in the **phloem**, from **sources** to **sinks**.
• A **source** is a region that RELEASES sucrose or amino acids — a photosynthesising leaf, or a storage organ mobilising its reserves in spring.
• A **sink** is a region that USES or STORES them — growing tips, young leaves, roots, developing fruits and seeds, and tubers filling with starch.

🔑 The key exam idea: the same organ can swap roles
A potato tuber is a SINK in summer (storing starch made from translocated sucrose) and a SOURCE in spring (breaking starch down to sucrose for the new shoots). A young, unfolding leaf is a sink; once mature it becomes a source. The direction of flow is therefore not fixed — it is set by which organs are sources and which are sinks at that moment.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 'glucose' as the transported sugar. The syllabus answer is **sucrose** (plus amino acids). Glucose is made in photosynthesis and converted to sucrose for transport. Also: translocation happens in the phloem, not the xylem — xylem carries water and mineral ions only.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Phloem moves sucrose and amino acids, source → sink.
• Source = releases; sink = uses or stores.
• Roles change with season and life stage — expect a question about a tuber or a fruit.

notes.heading: Photosynthesis: the Balanced Equation and Limiting Factors (Supplement 6.1)
notes.body:
📌 The balanced equation (Supplement 6.1.10)
The Core word equation becomes a balanced symbol equation — learn it exactly: **6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂**.
(Light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll. The basic equation, chlorophyll's role and the starch-test practical are in the Core photosynthesis topic.)

🔑 Identifying and EXPLAINING limiting factors (Supplement 6.1.11)
On a rate graph, the factor on the axis is limiting while the curve RISES; where the curve PLATEAUS, that factor is no longer limiting — something else is. Ask: which factor is in shortest supply here?
• Bright sun on a cold day → **temperature** limits.
• Warm, bright day in a still, unventilated greenhouse → **carbon dioxide** limits (the plants use it faster than it diffuses in).
• Dull winter day in a heated, CO₂-enriched greenhouse → **light intensity** limits.

💡 Worked Example — greenhouse economics
A grower heats a greenhouse and burns fuel to add CO₂. Both cost money, so the exam question is: which factor is limiting? On a dull winter day it is light — extra CO₂ gives little extra yield until artificial lighting (another cost) is added. Link the limiting factor to the ECONOMICS: only spend money raising a factor that is actually limiting.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 'the enzymes denature' to explain a plateau on a light or CO₂ graph. Over the normal range, rising temperature RAISES the rate; a plateau on a light or CO₂ graph means a DIFFERENT factor has become limiting, not that anything has denatured.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Balanced equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
• Rising slope = the axis factor is limiting; plateau = another factor is limiting.
• Greenhouse questions = limiting factors plus cost–benefit.

notes.heading: Tropic Responses: Core Description + the Auxin Mechanism (14.5)
notes.body:
📌 Definitions (Core 14.5.1)
• **Gravitropism** — a growth response to gravity: shoots grow AWAY from gravity (upwards) and roots grow TOWARDS gravity (downwards).
• **Phototropism** — a growth response to the direction of light: shoots grow TOWARDS the light.

🔑 Investigating tropisms (Core 14.5.2–3)
Typical practical: place seedlings on their side in the dark (gravity only), or upright with light from one side only. Shoots curve upwards / towards the light; roots curve downwards. Use several seedlings and repeat — a single seedling may be damaged or unusual. Keep light direction, orientation, water and temperature controlled, and compare with a control group in even light growing upright.

🔑 The auxin mechanism (Supplement 14.5.4–5) — chemical control of growth
Tropisms are an example of **chemical control of plant growth**, and the chemical is **auxin**:
1. Auxin is **made in the shoot tip**.
2. It **diffuses** back through the growing region.
3. Light from one side (or gravity, when the shoot is horizontal) makes auxin distribute **unequally** — it collects on the shaded side / the lower side.
4. In the shoot, the side with more auxin shows more **cell elongation**, so that side grows faster and the shoot bends — towards the light, or away from gravity.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying auxin 'attracts' the shoot towards the light, or that cells 'move towards the auxin'. Nothing travels except the direction of growth: unequal auxin → unequal cell elongation → curvature. Write the mechanism as the four steps above.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Gravitropism = response to gravity; phototropism = response to light direction.
• Investigate with groups of seedlings; control light direction and orientation.
• Auxin: made in the tip → diffuses → unequal distribution → unequal elongation → bending.

flashcards.definition: A measure of the tendency of water molecules to move. Pure water has the highest water potential; dissolving solutes lowers it.
flashcards.example: A concentrated salt solution has a lower water potential than distilled water, so water moves into it by osmosis.

flashcards.definition: The net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane.
flashcards.example: Water enters a plant cell from the soil because the soil water has a higher water potential than the cell sap.

flashcards.definition: The outward pressure of the swollen vacuole and cell contents on the cell wall when water has entered a plant cell by osmosis.
flashcards.example: Turgor pressure keeps non-woody stems upright and holds leaves flat.

flashcards.definition: The state of a plant cell that has lost turgor — no net water movement, vacuole not pressing on the wall, cell limp.
flashcards.example: A plant cell in a solution of equal water potential to its cell sap becomes flaccid.

flashcards.definition: Shrinkage of the vacuole until the cell membrane pulls away from the cell wall, caused by water leaving a plant cell by osmosis.
flashcards.example: Plant cells placed in concentrated salt solution become plasmolysed.

flashcards.definition: A tough, waterproof material thickening xylem walls; it strengthens the vessel against collapse under tension and stops water leaking out.
flashcards.example: Wood is mostly lignified xylem — that is why it is hard and strong.

flashcards.definition: The tension created by water evaporating from mesophyll surfaces, which draws water across the leaf and up the xylem.
flashcards.example: Transpiration pull, not pumping by the roots, moves water to the top of a tall tree.

flashcards.definition: Water molecules sticking together, so the transpiration pull is transmitted down the whole unbroken water column in the xylem.
flashcards.example: Because water is cohesive, one pull at the leaf moves the entire column from root to leaf.

flashcards.definition: The movement of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem, from sources to sinks.
flashcards.example: Sucrose made in a leaf is translocated to a developing fruit.

flashcards.definition: A source releases sucrose or amino acids into the phloem; a sink uses or stores them. The same organ can be both at different times.
flashcards.example: A potato tuber is a sink in summer and a source in spring.

flashcards.definition: A growth-controlling chemical made in the shoot tip; it diffuses through the growing region, is unequally distributed in response to light and gravity, and stimulates cell elongation.
flashcards.example: Auxin collecting on the shaded side of a shoot makes that side elongate more, bending the shoot towards the light.

flashcards.definition: Growth responses to gravity and light direction: shoots grow away from gravity and towards light; roots grow towards gravity.
flashcards.example: A seedling placed on its side curves its shoot upwards and its root downwards.

questions.stem: Which statement is the Supplement-level definition of osmosis?
choices: The movement of solute molecules from a concentrated solution into a dilute one
The movement of water from a dilute solution to a concentrated one by active transport
The net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane
The spreading of water molecules from where they are concentrated to where they are scarce, down a concentration gradient
questions.explanation: The Supplement definition names water potential and the partially permeable membrane. The 'concentration gradient' wording describes diffusion generally, solute movement is not osmosis, and osmosis is passive — never active transport.

questions.stem: How does dissolving solutes in water affect its water potential?
choices: It lowers the water potential
It raises the water potential
It has no effect on the water potential
It makes the water potential equal to that of pure water
questions.explanation: Pure water has the highest water potential, and adding solute lowers it. That is why a concentrated solution has a low water potential and draws water towards it by osmosis.

questions.stem: A plant cell is placed in a solution with a much LOWER water potential than its cell sap. What happens to the cell?
choices: It becomes turgid as water enters
It bursts because it has no cell wall
Nothing — the water potentials balance out instantly
Water leaves by osmosis; the vacuole shrinks and the membrane pulls away from the wall — the cell is plasmolysed
questions.explanation: Water moves from higher (cell sap) to lower (solution) water potential. Losing water shrinks the vacuole until the membrane leaves the wall — plasmolysis. Plant cells do not burst; the wall prevents that, and bursting is the animal-cell outcome.

questions.stem: A potato cylinder is weighed, left in distilled water for an hour, and weighed again. Its mass has increased. What is the explanation?
choices: Starch grains in the potato absorbed the water chemically
The distilled water had a higher water potential than the potato cell sap, so water entered the cells by osmosis
The potato cells respired and produced extra water
Salt moved out of the potato, which raised the cylinder's mass
questions.explanation: A mass gain means water entered the tissue, and water enters only when the surrounding solution has the higher water potential — distilled water has the highest possible. Losing salt would lower the mass, not raise it.

questions.stem: Which feature of xylem is correctly matched to its function?
choices: Sieve plates — allow sap to flow between the cells
No cross walls — the vessels form continuous tubes, so the water column is uninterrupted
Living cytoplasm — provides energy to pump the water upwards
Thin, unlignified walls — allow water to escape into the leaf
questions.explanation: Xylem cells are dead, with no contents and no end walls, forming continuous tubes. Sieve plates belong to phloem, xylem walls are lignified and waterproof, and water moves by transpiration pull rather than being pumped.

questions.stem: Why are xylem vessel walls thickened with lignin?
choices: To make the vessels flexible enough to bend with the stem
To make the walls permeable so mineral ions can enter
To strengthen and waterproof the walls so the vessel does not collapse under the tension of the transpiration pull
To store food reserves for the plant over winter
questions.explanation: Lignin is a tough, waterproof material. It reinforces the wall against the inward pull created when transpiration puts the water column under tension, and it prevents water leaking sideways out of the vessel.

questions.stem: On a humid, still day, the transpiration rate of a well-watered plant is low. Why?
choices: The water vapour gradient between the leaf's air spaces and the outside air is shallow, so diffusion out of the leaf is slow
The stomata are frozen shut by the moist air
High humidity makes the mesophyll cell walls waterproof
Still air means the xylem can no longer pull water upwards
questions.explanation: Transpiration is driven by diffusion down a water vapour gradient. Humid air outside (and no wind to clear it) keeps that gradient shallow, so water vapour leaves the leaf slowly. The xylem pull still works — it is the leaf end of the chain that slows.

questions.stem: Which statement about sources and sinks in translocation is correct?
choices: A source uses sucrose for growth while a sink releases it
Translocation always carries sucrose downwards, from leaves to roots
Translocation moves glucose and oxygen in the xylem
A potato tuber can be a sink in summer (storing starch) and a source in spring (supplying the new shoots)
questions.explanation: Sources release and sinks use or store, and an organ's role changes with the season — the tuber stores in summer and supplies in spring. Flow direction is not fixed, and translocation moves sucrose in the phloem, not the xylem.

questions.stem: A piece of potato neither gains nor loses mass when left in a salt solution for an hour. What does this show?
choices: The solution had a much higher water potential than the potato cells
The potato cells were dead, so no osmosis could occur
Osmosis happened, but the potato's skin stopped the mass changing
The solution had the same water potential as the potato cell sap, so there was no net movement of water
questions.explanation: No mass change means no net water movement, which happens when the two water potentials are equal — water molecules still cross the membrane, but at equal rates in both directions. Living cells and a partially permeable membrane are still required.

questions.stem: Wilting looks like pure damage, yet it can help a plant survive a hot, dry afternoon. How?
choices: Wilted leaves absorb more dew from the air
The collapsed leaves expose less surface to the sun, and flaccid guard cells close the stomata — both cut further water loss
Wilting reverses the direction of the transpiration stream
Wilting makes the xylem vessels widen, speeding up water uptake
questions.explanation: When transpiration exceeds uptake, cells lose turgor and the leaf sags. The hanging leaf catches less direct sunlight, and stomatal closure traps the remaining water vapour inside — wilting is partly a protective response, not just a failure.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes how the transpiration pull moves water up a tree?
choices: Root pressure pushes water up the xylem; evaporation in the leaves plays no part
Water molecules actively transport themselves up the xylem using ATP
Water evaporates from mesophyll surfaces, pulling more water across from the xylem; cohesion between water molecules transmits the pull down the continuous water column to the roots
Water diffuses up the phloem from the sinks to the sources
questions.explanation: Evaporation at the mesophyll surface is the engine: it pulls water from the xylem, and because water molecules cohere, the whole unbroken column is drawn up. The process is passive — no ATP — and it runs in the xylem, not the phloem.

questions.stem: On a graph of photosynthesis rate against light intensity, the curve rises and then levels off. What is limiting the rate along the flat part of the curve?
choices: A factor other than light — for example carbon dioxide concentration or temperature
Light intensity, because light is the factor on the axis
Chlorophyll, because the plant has run out of it
Oxygen, because it is a product of photosynthesis
questions.explanation: While the curve rises, the axis factor (light) is limiting. Once it plateaus, extra light has no effect, so something else — CO₂ or temperature — has become the limiting factor. A product such as oxygen cannot limit its own production.

questions.stem: The balanced equation for photosynthesis is __CO₂ + __H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + __O₂. Which set of coefficients is correct?
choices: 6, 6 and 6
1, 1 and 1
6, 6 and 1
2, 2 and 2
questions.explanation: 6CO₂ supplies 6 C and 12 O; 6H₂O supplies 12 H and 6 O — 18 oxygen atoms in total. The products C₆H₁₂O₆ (6 C, 12 H, 6 O) plus 6O₂ (12 O) balance both carbon, hydrogen and oxygen exactly.

questions.stem: A grower already heats the greenhouse and pumps in extra carbon dioxide, yet on dull winter days raising the CO₂ level further gives no extra yield. What is the best explanation?
choices: The plants have reached the maximum size their genes allow
CO₂ becomes toxic to the plants at high concentration
The burner used to make CO₂ uses up all the oxygen in the greenhouse
Light intensity is the limiting factor on dull days, so extra CO₂ cannot raise the rate — the grower is paying for a factor that is not limiting
questions.explanation: Increasing a non-limiting factor never raises the rate. On dull days light is in shortest supply, so money spent on extra CO₂ buys nothing until the lighting is improved — the classic greenhouse-economics application of limiting factors.

choices: A plant hormone carried in the xylem that causes cells to divide
A growth-controlling chemical made in the shoot tip, which diffuses through the growing region, is unequally distributed in response to light and gravity, and stimulates cell elongation
A pigment in the shoot tip that absorbs light for photosynthesis
An enzyme that digests the cell wall on one side of the shoot
questions.explanation: The Supplement mechanism is: made in the tip, diffuses back, becomes unequally distributed in response to light and gravity, and stimulates cell elongation — the unequal elongation is what bends the shoot. Auxin does not digest walls and is not a pigment.
